summary: At daybreak the whole council meets, questions Jesus again, condemns Him on His own words, and sends Him bound to Pilate.
key_insight: The council said, “we have heard it ourselves from His own mouth.” In the end they had no evidence except Jesus’ own testimony about who He is. He was condemned for telling the truth.
story: As soon as it was day, the elders of the people, both chief priests and scribes, came together {Lk} with the whole council. {Mk} They plotted against Jesus to put Him to death, {Mt} and they led Him into their council. {Lk}

“If You are the Christ, tell us,” they said. He answered, “If I tell you, you will by no means believe. And if I also ask you, you will by no means answer Me or let Me go. Hereafter the Son of Man will sit on the right hand of the power of God.” {Lk}

Then they all said, “Are You then the Son of God?” He said to them, “You rightly say that I am.” And they said, “What further testimony do we need? For we have heard it ourselves from His own mouth.” {Lk}
So they bound Jesus, led Him away, and delivered Him to Pilate. {Mk}
differences: Matthew and Mark mention the morning meeting in a single verse; only Luke gives the questions and answers.
Luke tells of no night trial. The questions he places at daybreak are like the ones Matthew and Mark place at the night hearing.
In Luke the council asks two separate questions, whether He is the Christ and whether He is the Son of God. Jesus answers, “You rightly say that I am.”
Only Luke records Jesus’ words, “If I tell you, you will by no means believe.”

fit.question: Matthew and Mark say the council questioned Jesus and condemned Him at night. Luke places the questioning at daybreak. Which is right?

points.label: Two sessions
points.text: Matthew and Mark tell of the night hearing and then say the council met again “when morning came” (Matthew 27:1; Mark 15:1). Luke leaves out the night hearing and tells only the morning session.

points.label: Why meet again
points.text: The night meeting was held in haste at the high priest’s house. A meeting by daylight gave the verdict formal standing and prepared the case for Pilate, who would hear it early in the morning.

points.label: The same question asked again
points.text: Asking the decisive question a second time made sure the verdict rested on Jesus’ own words “from His own mouth” (Luke 22:71). Luke’s order fits too: the guards’ mockery comes before the morning session, just where Matthew and Mark place it after the night verdict.

fit.note: Matthew and Mark themselves mention the morning meeting; Luke fills it in. The accounts complete each other.
fit.short: There were two sessions. Matthew and Mark tell the night hearing and mention the dawn meeting; Luke tells only the dawn meeting.

scene.label: First light
scene.text: Roman officials began their public business at first light, and governors heard cases early in the morning. If the council wanted Pilate to act that day, before the Sabbath began at sunset, they had to be at his door at dawn.

scene.label: A charge Rome would hear
scene.text: Blasphemy meant nothing under Roman law. But “the Christ” meant God’s anointed King, and a man called a king could be presented to Rome as a rival to Caesar. That is the charge the council took to Pilate (Luke 23:2).

scene.label: Where the council met
scene.text: Later Jewish tradition says the council met in a hall of the temple called the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and also that it had moved from there some years before the temple fell. Luke’s “into their council” may mean their meeting place or simply their assembly. Where this session met is uncertain.

witnesses.matthew: Gives one verse: the chief priests and elders “plotted against Jesus to put Him to death.” The decision made, Matthew turns at once to Judas, who sees that Jesus has been condemned (27:3).
witnesses.mark: Says it happened “immediately, in the morning” and that “the whole council” took part. Mark puts the responsibility on the full body, not on a few men acting at night.
witnesses.luke: Gives the session in full. Jesus does not say here that they will see Him coming, as in the night hearing, but that “hereafter” He “will sit on the right hand of the power of God.” His exaltation begins from the very hour of His rejection.

seeing.reveals: Jesus knew His judges would neither believe Him nor answer Him, yet He told them the truth: from now on the Son of Man sits at the right hand of God’s power.
seeing.living: Jesus did not argue to win the room; He testified and left the verdict with God. When people have already decided not to hear, you can still say what is true about Jesus plainly and without bitterness, and trust the One who sits at God’s right hand.
seeing.ponder: Are there truths about Jesus you have heard clearly, but have already decided not to believe?

preaching.big_idea: They heard the truth from His own mouth, and still refused Him.
outline: A question asked without wanting an answer (66–68)
A claim to God’s right hand (69)
A confession turned into a verdict (70–71)
preaching.watch_for: “Hereafter” (v. 69) marks a turning point: from this hour the condemned Jesus is the enthroned Son of Man. Later, before the same council, Stephen saw Him “standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56).
